toc.title: 5. Take a warm bath or shower

blocks.p: If you're struggling with daily anxiety, you need immediate skills to manage the experience and get you to a functional baseline, so you can stop ruminating, worrying, and expecting the worst. These seven are the easier ones: the more approachable skills that don't cost anything, or very little.

From a polyvagal perspective, anxiety is the emotional, conscious experience of the body's impulse to escape. When you don't act on your body's impulse to escape, anxiety emerges as that impulse lingers in the system.

Say you're someone who doesn't do well with social situations. You don't like workplace potlucks, meeting new people, being in large groups, or going somewhere crowded, like a mall on Christmas Eve. If you're that kind of person, like I am, you're going to have an impulse to leave that situation, whether it's a workplace potluck or a meeting that could have been an email. But maybe you can't, because of social norms or the expectations of the workplace. If you can't act on the impulse to leave, that flight activation lingers in your system, and you experience it more consciously as anxiety.

These skills are about managing anxiety, not curing it. I do believe anxiety can get a hell of a lot better, and as a therapist, I see that very often. But that's not a guarantee here, and it's not what we're aiming for. This is about reducing the intensity of your anxiety and getting you to a more functional baseline.

There are tons of things you can do to manage anxiety, and I don't know you in particular. So read through these seven and pick the ones that are approachable, the ones you can actually, practically use starting now. Here they are:

ol: Take a warm bath or shower.

blocks.p: Deep breathing can be a really simple and effective way to reduce anxiety.

ol: Sit comfortably. I recommend sitting upright.
Take a deep breath in through your nose, into your belly.
Hold it for a few seconds, just a slight pause.
Exhale slowly through your mouth. The slower exhale is really the key.

blocks.p: I did a bit of research, and found one study and a meta-analysis of studies showing that deep or belly breathing improved sustained attention, affect, and cortisol levels. It also increased comfort, relaxation, pleasantness, vigor, and alertness, and reduced symptoms of arousal, anxiety, depression, anger, and confusion. So belly breathing has a lot of benefits.

With anxiety in particular, that extended exhale uses the parasympathetic system, which calms the body and slows your heart. Slowing the heartbeat is exactly what's needed when you're anxious, because anxiety comes from a flight impulse, a polyvagal state of sympathetic flight, and an increased heart rate comes along with it. If you can get your heartbeat to slow down a bit, that should help lower your anxiety. I think mindful breathing can be really helpful here, especially with that extended exhale.
When should you use breathing exercises? In my opinion, breath can be used for any level of anxiety intensity, even panic attacks. But it's not easy, and you'll get better results if:

ul: You practice these breathing exercises ahead of time, before there's a problem, before there's intense anxiety.
You have a high distress tolerance, which you can build by strengthening your vagal brake, the strength of your polyvagal safety state.
You've practiced mindfulness and can attune to your breath.

blocks.p: Practice is a big part of this, and practice increases the strength of your safety state. If the safety state is stronger, the defensive states, flight, fight, shutdown, and freeze, won't be as intense.

Taking short breaks to stretch and move your body can help reduce tension and promote relaxation. I recommend mindful stretching and movement over using your phone to distract yourself from anxiety, which I know a lot of us go to.

How does movement help? When you use movement mindfully, it uses up that pent-up flight energy lingering in the system. It also reminds your body that movement is possible and that you're not actually immobilized. When you feel anxiety and you're immobilized, not moving, it makes things worse. Your body needs movement, even fidgeting. Fidgeting can help too.

I'd recommend using movement when you notice your anxiety escalating, but not out of control yet, and when you can take a break from whatever you're doing. At work, I make it a habit to get up and walk around the block once a day, just to go out and feel the air, and the sunshine if it's out, as long as it's not too hot. It gets me moving, and it gets me away from my desk and my monitor, which I really need.

I highly recommend combining movement with being mindful of the sensory experience of your environment: what you feel on your skin, what you hear, what you see. Be mindful of that while you move, and it can really help you manage anxiety.
Music can be really, really helpful. Choose a piece of music you find soothing and relaxing, something that helps you breathe a bit easier or lets you slow down and feel more present.

There's another route you could take: music that helps you mobilize and feel playful. Choose music that feeds into the mobilization of anxiety and listen to it in a playful, dancing, rhythmic way. Or listen to music that helps you slow down and breathe a bit easier.
Music can help lower anxiety in a bunch of ways:

ul: It can help you move, through dance.
It provides a rhythm to synchronize with, and helps you feel more present.

There might be vocal prosody in it, the singsongy quality of the voice. If you're listening to rap or heavy metal, there won't be a whole lot of vocal prosody, but where it's there, it helps. It's a cue of safety to your system, telling your body that what you're listening to is safe. It's a co-regulation thing.
It may match the intensity of what you're feeling, and that allows the feeling to be present within you, if you can sustain it or tolerate it.
It can also function as a distraction. If you just need to distract yourself and you can't really mindfully experience it, that's fine too. Again, we're managing the anxiety, not getting rid of it.

blocks.p: Personally, I think music is kind of always a good idea for reducing anxiety. You can have it on in the background, and it provides a passive cue of safety, reminding your system that you're safe. At work, just put some earbuds in. That can be very discreet. Or if you're with friends and you want to dance it out, go right ahead. That's not really my style, but it can be a really good co-regulating, social way to be mobile and to play.
Writing in a journal can help you process your thoughts and emotions, which helps reduce anxiety. Take a few minutes each day and write down your thoughts and feelings.

Specifically, I recommend focusing on the present moment, not on the past, especially the more painful things. I don't need you to reflect on what you've been through and conjure up those past thoughts and feelings. Focusing on your present-moment thoughts and emotions can be more helpful.

Journaling can help you align your cognitions, the words in your head, the images, the memories, with what's happening within you from the bottom up. It also helps you align with the external world. If you journal about the present moment, you might write about:

ul: What your senses are detecting, like sights and sounds.
Your present-moment emotional experience, like anxiousness or nervousness.
What it feels like to be in the present moment, journaling.

blocks.p: If you can get your thoughts to align with the present moment through journaling, that gives your anxiety permission to be present. You're not ignoring it. You're letting it be there, aligning with it, and experiencing it on some level, but in a tolerable way. And you're getting it out of your system, in a way, instead of letting it linger there. That can reduce its intensity.

If you want to go further, and you're allowing your anxious feelings to be there while you journal, use the speed of your writing to feel the anxiety more, in a tolerable and safe way. If you feel really jittery and fast-paced, let yourself write in a jittery, fast-paced way. You could also just doodle, sketch, or scribble. It doesn't have to be coherent written words.

I think journaling is best done when the anxious feelings are mild to moderate. It really helps to stay anchored in the present moment. Feelings and memories connected to past events might come up while you journal, and staying anchored in the present moment raises your ability to tolerate them, be curious about them, and let them be there.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: 5. Take a warm bath or shower

blocks.p: You might add some Epsom salts or essential oils to enhance the relaxation. Bathing provides numerous passive cues of safety to your system, which help lower your flight activation and your anxiety: the warmth of the water on your skin, the scents of soaps or oils, maybe the solitude of being alone in the bathroom. Personally, I think just feeling clean is a cue of safety too.

Those passive safety cues can also be actively noticed and experienced. If you set yourself up with a relaxing scene, you can mindfully experience it. Slow down and really take the cues in, maybe one by one. Notice what it feels like to have warmth on your skin, all over your body. Notice how your body reacts to the scent you've chosen. That's how you take passive cues of safety and actively experience them.

One of my therapy clients took a two-hour bath every night as part of her bedtime routine, with a charcuterie board: cheeses, meats. I don't recommend this exactly, but it does sound amazing. I think I would love that.

I do highly recommend daily bathing. Please do that. But think of this one as part of your daily structure, more preventative than a coping skill. It's an opportunity every day to feel more relaxation, more slowness, more warmth, and more solitude. It's a way to start or end your day calmly, a foundational piece of your daily structure. You could use it as a coping skill, but I recommend it more as a preventative thing.

Teas, including green tea and chamomile, can potentially help reduce anxiety, and I found a couple of studies that support that idea. Unfortunately, tea isn't free, though it's pretty darn cheap. This one might be less accessible if you don't have any tea money to splurge on.

How does tea help? There might be benefits from the ingredients themselves, like the herbs, or maybe the caffeine. But for me, it's the taste, the warmth, the scent. Tea is a really great source of passive safety cues. The scent, the sight of it, and the warmth provide cues of safety that are relaxing without you having to do anything besides drink the tea.
You can also mindfully attune to these cues and get even more benefit by asking yourself, "What's it like for me to drink this tea, and smell it, and taste it?"

I recommend drinking tea when you have a decent amount of anchoring in your safety state and can really be mindful of the experience. If you're super anxious, messing around with hot water might not be a great idea. Especially if you're in a panic attack and you're jittery, you might not want to mess with scalding hot water. But with mild to moderate anxiety or stress, I think tea is a really good option, as long as you can mindfully take it in. I don't think it's as helpful if it's mindless, if you're just chugging tea.
Hold on here, because I'm not saying go to a forest. You could actually be in nature, yes, but it could also be elements of nature. Something nature-ish, I'll put it that way.

You could go to a forest or a national park and be there for the day, taking it in, in solitude and quiet. Lovely. If you can do that, go right ahead, hiking or biking through it or whatever. But maybe there's a park near your house you could walk around. It's not the same, but there's grass and there are birds, and that's close enough. Or maybe you can just hang out in your backyard.

One evening, I was barbecuing and just sat on the deck in the backyard. It wasn't too hot, but it was sunny. It was evening, but not too dark. It was breezy, but not too windy. It was just right, a peaceful scene with elements of nature I could just take in.

Maybe you don't even have access to that. Maybe you live in a noisy apartment on the fifth floor. Maybe you can put potted plants in your apartment. It's not a forest, a backyard, or a park, but it's an element of nature. Having those greens present really helps.

Here's how I conceptualize it. Everything evolved in nature, humans included. I think we generally feel an aversion to the dangerous elements of nature, like lightning and hail. We typically don't want to go out into those. But we're drawn to the safer aspects of nature, like water and greenery. Safety can include a warm sun, a gentle breeze, quiet solitude. Hearing birds singing also indicates that there's no danger present. So when you have these elements of nature in your life, they're naturally a cue of safety.

I even use fake plants in my therapy offices, and that's better than none. During sessions, I'll also have my computer monitor playing a long nature scene: someone recording their walk through a forest, or a camera set up on a waterfall for twenty minutes, on a loop. My clients' eyes gravitate toward it, and they can really settle into it. It's not real, it's a monitor, but it's better than nothing.

I recommend using nature as often as you can. If you don't have a lake or a whimsical fairytale forest nearby, that's okay. Use elements of nature. If you can bring them into your life and your space, they passively increase your cues of safety, which reduces your flight activation, which reduces your anxious feelings.
Find one or two or three of these that you can begin to do now.
